analysis.one_liner: Makes repeal of the federal estate tax on large inherited estates permanent.
analysis.headline: The House passed the estate-tax repeal 272-162, but the Senate never began debate — a vote to start considering it fell 57-41, three short of the 60 needed.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 Bush tax law eliminated the federal estate tax, but only until the end of 2010, after which the tax was set to come back automatically. This bill would strike that expiration date, making repeal of the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes permanent. The estate tax applies only to very large inherited estates; it touches a small fraction of deaths, concentrated among the wealthiest families.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates, who would never owe estate tax on inherited wealth. Only estates above a high exemption — then several million dollars per person — owe the tax at all, so the benefit is concentrated among the wealthiest inheritances.

how_it_helps.text: Permanently repeals the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes by removing the 2010 sunset in the 2001 tax law [S2][S4].
Removes the risk that heirs to large family businesses or farms would owe the tax after it returns in 2011 — the main argument supporters gave [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. Repealing the estate tax permanently removes a revenue stream that comes entirely from the largest estates, forcing other taxes to fill the gap or adding to deficits.

drawbacks.text: The permanent revenue loss is borne by the general federal budget, since the tax is owed only by the largest estates — the benefit goes to a small number of the wealthiest inheritances while the cost is spread across everyone [S2].

Supporters argued the tax forces surviving spouses or heirs to sell family farms and small businesses to pay the bill, and that it taxes wealth a person may already have paid tax on while earning it — a real objection even though the bill's benefit is concentrated at the top.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it goes almost entirely to estates large enough to owe the tax, which is a small share of all deaths. The cost — a permanent loss of federal revenue — is spread across all taxpayers through other taxes or larger deficits. A permanent repeal with no offsetting revenue was weighted heavily toward the very wealthiest households.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it easily, but the Senate never even began debating it — a procedural vote just to start considering the bill fell three votes short of the 60 needed, and the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill would remove the 2010 sunset in the 2001 tax law so the estate tax repeal never expires [S2][S4].
It drew 206 cosponsors, including 190 Republicans and 16 Democrats [S5].
The House passed it 272-162 on April 13, 2005, with 230 of 232 Republicans and 42 of 202 Democrats in favor [S7][S6].
The Senate never took it up: cloture on the motion to proceed — the vote just to begin considering the bill — failed 57-41 on June 8, 2006, three votes short of the 60 required [S8][S6].
The bill died with the 109th Congress, and the estate tax returned in 2011 as scheduled [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the federal treasury kept the estate tax on the largest estates after it returned in 2011. Heirs to very large estates did not get the permanent repeal they sought — though the temporary repeal was still in effect through 2010.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was 230-1 among Republicans and split 42-160 among Democrats; in the Senate, 53 of 55 Republicans voted to proceed while 38 of 44 Democrats voted no, with the four Democratic yes votes not enough.

industries.note: The estate tax falls only on estates above a multi-million-dollar exemption, so permanent repeal hands a lasting tax cut to the largest inheritances, funded by the general federal budget. Ordinary taxpayers bear the revenue loss through other taxes or higher deficits [S2].

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory services
industries.note: A permanent estate tax creates steady demand for trust, valuation, and estate-planning work by wealthy families; repeal would take away that business. The industry's interest in keeping the tax runs against the few families who owe it.
